query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of the high-entropy alloy is governed by the dynamic formation and partial mechanical removal of a continuous high-entropy spinel oxide layer, which simultaneously resists wear via its inherent hardness and protects against corrosion by acting as a passivating barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited equiatomic HEA (20% Fe, 20% Co, 20% Ni, 20% Mn, 20% Cu) on an SS-304 substrate without a pre-formed protective oxide film.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA coating to a tribo-corrosion testing environment where both mechanical sliding (wear) and a corrosive medium are applied concurrently.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under moderate load and sliding speed in an oxidative electrolyte at elevated temperatures similar to those found in SOFC interconnect applications, where oxidation kinetics promote the formation of spinel oxides.
generation.structural_mediator: A high-entropy spinel oxide film (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 that forms in situ through thermal oxidation and is subject to cyclic removal and reformation during wear.
generation.mechanism: During tribo-corrosion, the ambient conditions favor rapid formation of a protective high-entropy spinel oxide film. Under mechanical wear, portions of this film are removed, exposing fresh alloy surface that quickly re-oxidizes back into the spinel. This dynamic balance between film removal and reformation ultimately controls both the extent of mechanical damage and the rate of corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline HEA lacking the rapid spinel formation capability (e.g., through a processing modification), the alloy exhibiting the dynamic spinel oxide layer will show lower total degradation with reduced wear depth and lower corrosion current. The combined protective effect should yield a synergistic improvement in durability under concurrent tribological and corrosive stresses.
generation.baseline: A matched high-entropy alloy system processed such that the formation of the high-entropy spinel oxide (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 is suppressed, serving as the control for tribo-corrosion degradation.
generation.boundary: The prediction should hold under conditions that allow for meaningful oxide reformation (moderate wear rates, sufficient oxidation environment, and temperatures high enough to promote oxide kinetics) but may fail in extreme wear conditions where the oxide is removed too rapidly or in inert environments that do not support oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide film reformation under varying loads and sliding speeds, and the effect of microstructural heterogeneities on film integrity and adhesion, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one high-entropy alloy processed to favor high-entropy spinel oxide formation and a baseline sample modified (e.g., by slight compositional tweaks or process variations) to hinder oxide film formation. Subject both sets to identical tribo-corrosion tests with controlled mechanical wear and exposure to a corrosive, oxidizing medium at elevated temperatures. Assess changes in surface morphology, oxide film thickness, wear track depth, and corrosion current.
measurements: Surface analysis using SEM/EDS to characterize oxide film continuity and thickness
Wear track depth and volume loss measurements
Electrochemical corrosion testing (e.g., corrosion current densities)
Hardness measurements before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sample designed to promote spinel oxide formation does not show a statistically significant reduction in both wear and corrosion rates compared to the baseline sample, or if no evidence of a dynamic oxide film (periodic removal and reformation) is observed on the worn surfaces, the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
Deposition of high entropy alloy FeCoNiMnCu on SS-304 was carried out by microwave energy for application in “solid oxide fuel-cell (SOFC) interconnects”. The ball-milling has been performed by taking “Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu” in equal 20 wt. % of before deposited on SS-304 substrate. The deposited steel with 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu high entropy alloy (HEA) was exposed to thermal-exposure in the air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C. The uniform cladding distribution of 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu HEA particles can be apparently observed on SS-304 substrate by utilizing Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM), and Optical microscopy analysis. Homogeneity in the interfacial layer was evident by employing Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) characterization. Results have indicated that after the thermal exposure of deposited steel with 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu in the air for up to ten weeks at 800 °C, a “protective Cr2O3 layer”, and “high-entropy spinel coating” of (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 have been formed.
